15.0.0.en: I saw another sign: that is, a new vision, other than the seven churches, the seven seals, the seven trumpets and the vision of the dragon and the two beasts. He affirms that it is great and marvelous because of the scenes and meanings it contains. Seven angels .. seven plagues: the number seven points to the perfection and severity of these plagues. They are not like the earlier plagues, for those were for discipline and for man's turning back from his evil, whereas these are for stern punishment.

15.0.1.en: The last: pointing to the fact that they come immediately before the judgment and nothing follows them ... in them all the wrath and vengeance of God is completed.

15.0.2.en: St. John saw a great sight: seven angels carrying seven bowls, which are the wrath of God, before the day of judgment.

15.1.0.en: I saw a sea of glass: this is the same sea that is before the divine throne (ch. 4:6). Glass and crystal signify purity and transparency, for no one can stand in the presence of God unless he is pure and clean.

15.1.1.en: Mingled with fire: fire signifies the divine justice that pierces, examines and repays. In another interpretation, this fire may point to the sufferings that the children of God pass through during their lives, which qualify them to stand before Him. And them that had gotten the victory over the beast: that is, those who completed the race and the striving and triumphed over Satan and all his marks and followers, and did not submit or bow down to him. See what was said about the marks of the beast and his image (ch. 13). Having the harps of God: that is, God gave them the spirit of prayer and praise, and this is their new angelic work.

15.1.2.en: In this verse he reassures us, before mentioning God's wrath in the bowls, with a beautiful sight: the children of God who believe in Him, who have triumphed over Satan and stand in purity around the throne of God praising Him.

15.2.0.en: They sing the song of Moses: when Moses crossed the Red Sea and Pharaoh was drowned, Moses praised God, offering Him glorification and thanksgiving (Ex 15:1-19). This is what the Church now also chants in the first Hos (praise) of the Midnight Praise ... So the victors here sing a song similar to what Moses uttered.

15.2.1.en: The song of the Lamb: that is, this praise is offered to Christ the Redeemer as it is to His Father.

15.2.2.en: As for the content of this praise, it is the confession of the greatness of God's dispensation in all His works, and rejoicing in His infinite power, and that all His commandments, promises and covenants are true, and that He reigns over the hearts of His holy children, that is, those who have consecrated their hearts to Him.

15.3.0.en: Who shall not fear thee, O Lord, and glorify thy name: in their praise they also confess the awesomeness of the person of God and the power of His name. For the gentle, calm, longsuffering God who loves mankind is Himself the God whom Isaiah, when he saw Him in his vision, cried out, saying, "Woe is me, for I am a man of unclean lips" (Isa 6:5). All nations shall come and worship before thee: all people without exception (the wicked and the righteous) will submit to You and worship before You on the day of judgment, and will declare that You alone are worthy of worship and no other (not the beast, to whom the wicked bowed down before). The worship of the wicked is not adoration but fear and terror of the wrath that is coming upon them.

15.3.1.en: Thy judgments are made manifest: that is, Your justice has been completed and You have proclaimed Your judgments, and what was not understood has become plain and clear, and You have revealed it to us.

15.3.2.en: The children of God complete their glorification of Him on the day of judgment, proclaiming His holiness and fear, and the submission of all mankind to Him, after the perfection of His mercy toward His children and His justice in the judgment of the wicked has appeared.

15.4.0.en: And after that: an expression used often, by which St. John moves us from one scene to another.

15.4.1.en: The tabernacle of the testimony: this is the tabernacle of meeting, and it was given this name because it contained the tablets of the Law, "the testimony." Stephen also used this name (Acts 7:44). St. John saw a vision of the tabernacle of meeting, but in heaven, and its temple signifies the divine presence and will. The going out of the seven angels means that they went out charged with a majestic divine command. The description of what these angels wore agrees with the garments of the priests in the Old Testament, "linen," which signifies purity and cleanness; and they also resemble the splendor of their God, who appeared girt with a golden girdle (ch. 1:13), because He is the one High Priest, and their clothing like what He wears means that they represent Him and carry out His will.

15.5.0.en: One of the angels who are near to God and always present before Him (one of the four living creatures) gave the seven angels seven bowls, and they are of gold, pointing to the fact that their source is from God and that they represent His justice and His wrath against the wicked.

15.5.1.en: The bowl: a concave vessel, used for putting incense and offering it during worship.

15.6.0.en: The temple was filled with smoke: this has no relation to the bowls, for the bowls carried divine wrath, whereas this smoke is one of the manifestations of the glory of God ... as happened when Moses received the tablets of the Law, and the mountain smoked like a furnace (Ex 19:18); likewise at the dedication of the temple in the days of Solomon the same smoke settled on the temple (1 Kgs 8:11), and when Isaiah saw the Lord (Isa 6..). Because of the density of this smoke, that is, the greatness of God's glory and power, no one could look or enter until God's dispensation and decree were fulfilled in carrying out His seven plagues through His angels.

15.6.1.en: Great is Your glory, O Lord ... who is able to describe it or stand before it!!...

15.6.2.en: But You have granted us not only to stand but to speak with You and to call You our Father ... So teach us also, my Lord, that the sight of Your most holy glory may not be absent from our eyes, so that we pray to You with reverence and contrition and keep our minds under control before You during prayer ... Forgive us, my God, for we often forget!!! The seven bowls of God's wrath: a general introduction to the chapter: this chapter comes as a continuation of what chapter fifteen indicated (the plagues of the seven angels), and here it describes them in detail. In these seven plagues the following is noted:

15.6.3.en: First: their resemblance to a great extent to the ten plagues with which God struck the Egyptians, with the difference that they are symbolic and carry spiritual meanings, whereas the ten plagues were, as God spoke them, entirely real.

15.6.4.en: Second: they also resemble the seven doors, which likewise carried plagues and vengeance, but they are more severe than the plagues of the trumpets (Rev 6-8).

16.0.0.en: Bowls: plural of bowl, and the bowl is a vessel resembling a cup.

16.0.1.en: St. John heard the command issued to begin carrying out, that is, to pour out these plagues (the bowls) on the earth. He describes the voice as great, to indicate the severity of the events that follow, and the coming of this voice out of the temple means that it represents the divine will.

16.1.0.en: And the first went: that is, the first of the angels holding the bowls.

16.1.1.en: A noisome sore: that is, incurable and unknown to physicians.

16.1.2.en: After the command was given to the angels, the first carried it out, and his plague covered the earth, but it did not strike all its inhabitants, only those who followed Satan and departed from the way of divine truth. This plague of sores resembles the sixth plague with which God struck the Egyptians, and the resemblance increases in that it did not strike everyone who was in the land of Egypt, but those who bore the mark of "Pharaoh," that is, the idolaters, while the people of God were kept safe from it. The sores point to agitation and anxiety, for their spread over the body takes away its rest; likewise their foul smell points to the blasphemies of the people who have the image of the beast. The most severe thing about this plague is that it is a plague without cure, and how terrible it is for a man to suffer a pain for which there is no healing and no end.

16.1.3.en: My God, is this not what really happens to everyone who leaves the way and bows down to the beast, that is, gives himself up to the world and its authority and its pleasures, so that the result is anxiety, weariness and pain that has no end except by returning to Your embrace and enjoying Your presence .. I thank You, my God, because to everyone who lives with You You have given immunity from such painful plagues.

16.2.0.en: This plague reminds us of the plague of the second trumpet, which took a third of the sea only (ch. 8:8), but here, because of its severity, the plague covered the sea and everything in it.

16.2.1.en: The sea: points to the world, troubled in its thoughts and deeds.

16.2.2.en: It became blood: the worst sight, which the human soul shrinks from looking at.

16.2.3.en: As the blood of a dead man: that is, congealed blood that has lost life and the self-movement it carries, and therefore it is clotted and putrid blood.

16.2.4.en: Every living soul .. died: what is meant is the people whom the world sweeps along in its currents, who bear no spiritual identity and did not respond to God and His calls.

16.2.5.en: The divine inspiration uses the images most cruel to the soul to depict the state of those upon whom God's wrath comes .. and the first purpose of this hard description is to move people to repentance and return, so that they may have deliverance from these woes.

16.3.0.en: What happened in the sea also covered all the rivers, which always signify the sources of life, as if God wants to tell us that death will be general, covering everything. This plague reminds us of the first plague with which God struck Pharaoh and the land of Egypt as well (Ex 7:19). Perhaps also the rivers and springs point to the heretics, who were at first a spring of sound teaching and faith, then deviated and began to offer poisoned water and teaching contrary to what the Church received, and for this reason they deserved the bowl of God's wrath.

16.4.0.en: For they have shed ..: the words here refer to the followers of the beast who bear his mark and persecute the Church of God, or to the heretics who wearied the Church with their heresies.

16.4.1.en: Because of the difficulty and severity of this plague, the words came on the tongue of the angel, showing that what happened was connected with the absolute justice of God and His eloquence, and the angel's words came in the form of:

16.4.2.en: 1- Praise of the name of God: for he glorified God, the eternal and everlasting One, and highlighted the attribute of His absolute justice in His judgments.

16.4.3.en: 2- A clarification that what happens to the wicked is what they truly deserve, and that the punishment came in the same kind as the wrong (v. 8); and because they shed blood, they were given blood to drink, "for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap" (Gal 6:7).

16.4.4.en: 3- Confession (v. 7:), that is, the rest of the heavenly creation, in the person of the other angel, declared its faith in what the first angel uttered, that God is the true and just One in all His judgments and repays each one according to his deserving, and although He is longsuffering toward the wicked, His punishment remains for the one who does not repent.

16.4.5.en: My God and good Savior, no sooner do my eyes fall upon the words that speak of Your justice and Your recompense than I find myself trembling, remembering my sins, and nothing rescues me from this except remembering Your very wide mercies toward everyone who seeks them ... and therefore I cry out with all the people of Your Church, "According to Your mercy, O Lord, and not according to our sins."

16.5.0.en: The sun is supposed to be a source of warmth, light and joy, as it is one of the essentials of life, but it turned into an instrument of burning and severe pain. The meaning intended by this is that everything that was a cause of blessing, pride or comfort .. became a cause of pain and distress. The fire here is figurative, for it is not reasonable that one who was greatly burned should still be alive and blaspheme the name of God. But this applies even more to the material goods that God gives to man, yet because people are immersed in them and preoccupied with them, they turn into a burning, disturbing fire that robs them of their peace and even consumes and devours them, so they forget God; and instead of returning to Him and confessing their sins so that the blessing might return to them, they blaspheme His name and reject Him, and so their gloom and distress increase and they suffer by them.

16.6.0.en: The fifth divine vengeance came directed at the kingdom of the beast himself, which is every power opposed to the Kingdom of Christ. And because they are the very kingdom of darkness, God's vengeance on them was to strike them with more darkness, so that they become like blind men stumbling about. And to show the severity of their pains from this plague, the inspired text portrays them as "gnawing their tongues," for it is known that biting the tongue is very painful to a person, so how great must the pain be that makes a man bite his tongue?!

16.7.0.en: Like all the preceding ones, this plague did not bring them to repentance; on the contrary, they went from darkness to the pain of "sores," and from pain to despair, so they blasphemed the name of the Most High God.

16.7.1.en: I wish, my brother, that you would use the world but not let it rule over you, nor cling to it. Do not give yourself all that you desire, and use everything in measure, even if you have the ability to buy and possess all you want. Here the importance of fasting and keeping to it appears, for it helps you to control yourself so that these desires do not enslave you, and the devil is unable to fight you with them, so that you have deliverance from these plagues that strike the wicked who are immersed in the world.

16.8.0.en: Babylon was the kingdom of evil that took captive and enslaved the people of God, and it became in the Holy Bible a symbol of all evil and its power. Here the divine wrath came directed at its most famous river (the Euphrates), the cause of its pride and its prosperity, and God dried it up, that is, He confined its glory, pointing to the beginning of its passing away and the end of its iniquity. The kings of the east: after God removed the glory of Babylon by drying up its river (the Euphrates), there come out from God, that is, from the East, kings who reign in place of Babylon, and this is what happened when the kingdom of the Medes and Persians removed the Babylonian empire, and it will happen at the end when Christ reigns after He removes the kingdom of Satan.

16.9.0.en: It is noted that verses 15-16 depict a parenthetical scene between the sixth bowl and the seventh bowl.

16.9.1.en: The dragon .. the beast .. the false prophet: these are the three powers that Satan uses, who were mentioned in (ch. 13), but the second beast (ch. 13:11) is renamed here "the false prophet." St. John saw Satan here in a new form that indicates his characteristics all the more, since there came out of the mouths of the three, three unclean spirits in the form of frogs .. Why frogs, then ...?! Only because they represent Satan in the best possible way:

16.9.2.en: 1- Frogs are found in pools and in muddy, miry places (for this is the place and standing of Satan.)

16.9.3.en: 2- The frog is an animal ugly in color and form.

16.9.4.en: 3- The frog is a nocturnal animal whose home and place is always the darkness.

16.9.5.en: 4- The frog is an animal whose voice (its croaking) disturbs and troubles the people who hear it (as Satan does with the children of God.)

16.10.0.en: These demons go out with signs and wonders that reach the point of miracles, and they know that this is their last war (especially after the river Euphrates has dried up), so they strive to gather all their children, the wicked rulers of this world, to fight the children of God in their last war with them.

16.10.1.en: That great day: it is the day of God's just and final judgment, that is, the day of judgment.

16.10.2.en: God Almighty: that is, whatever Satan does, the victory belongs to God alone.

16.11.0.en: Behold, I come as a thief: the words here are the Lord Christ's, and they mean that He comes suddenly and without any fixed time for His coming.

16.11.1.en: Keepeth his garments: that is, prepared, wearing the garments of virtue and righteousness.

16.11.2.en: Lest he walk naked: that is, whoever Christ finds unprepared at the time of His coming will be exposed before people, and they will see his shame.

16.11.3.en: This verse is parenthetical between verses 15-16, and it is a call from Christ to all His followers to watch and be prepared to meet Him at any time.

16.11.4.en: Understand, O my soul, that dreadful day, and awake and trim your lamp with the oil of gladness, for you do not know when the voice will come to you saying, Behold, the Bridegroom has come. So take heed, O my soul, do not slumber, lest you stand outside like the five foolish virgins, but watch, entreating, that you may meet Christ the Lord ... and He may grant you the wedding feast of His true divine glory) ... from the prayers of the Agpeya.(

16.12.0.en: And he gathered them together: that is, Satan with his unclean spirits gathered all his followers and his armies.

16.12.1.en: Armageddon: a Hebrew word meaning the mountain of Megiddo, a mountain well known to the Jews that witnessed various historical events, such as the victory of the judges Gideon, Barak and Deborah. Since Satan knew that the end of his work on earth was near, he gathered all his energies for the last war. Of course "Armageddon" here does not point to a specific place, for the war is not material, but it points to the final battle and the defeat of Satan and his last judgment.

16.13.0.en: When the seventh angel poured out the last bowl of God's wrath, heaven declared that the seven bowls were completed.

16.13.1.en: Into the air: that is, upon the kingdom of Satan, who considered the air his dwelling and his authority (Eph 2:2). It is done: equivalent to the word "It is finished" that the Savior uttered on the Cross, and in agreement with the phrase "for in them is filled up the wrath of God" (Rev 15:1).

16.14.0.en: The expression "thunders, and lightnings, and an earthquake" is repeated in several places in the Book of Revelation, such as (ch. 8:5), (ch. 11:19), and they all accompanied important events. But here, because the end has drawn near, St. John makes clear that nothing like it or equal to its power had occurred before, nor one like its violence in all the age of mankind since its creation.

16.15.0.en: The great city: some saw it as Babylon, because it symbolizes evil, and some saw it as Jerusalem, where Christ was crucified, but in its spiritual meaning it is the kingdom of Satan, of which he boasts. Three parts: that is, it collapsed, was scattered and lost its power, and the number three represents perfection, that is, its ruin was complete.

16.15.1.en: Great Babylon: it signifies here the center of the great city and the place of the throne and seat of Satan. The effect of this great earthquake, or of the last cup of God's wrath, was the collapse of the kingdom of evil and the fall of its power, and Satan himself fell, and likewise all his followers fell, that is, the cities of the nations. But Babylon, which signifies the center of evil and the throne of Satan, was mentioned separately, to make clear that God had another purpose concerning her final, doubled punishment, expressed by "the cup of the wine of the fierceness of his wrath," an expression which as a whole means the wrath stored up by God throughout the days (like aged wine) against evil and its kingdom.

16.16.0.en: This verse is a continuation and clarification of the picture of the violent earthquake, the like of which has not occurred on the earth, for the islands fled away, meaning they were covered with water and disappeared, and the mountains were not found, meaning the dissolution of the elements of the earth and the beginning of the disappearance of its known geographical features.

16.17.0.en: A great hail: like the plague of hail on the land of Egypt (Ex 9:18-25). It means the falling of snow with frost.

16.17.1.en: The weight of a talent: about (17.5 kg), and the meaning intended is its great heaviness upon the people.

16.17.2.en: The perfection of this plague came in that God sent down upon the people hail the like of which the world had not known before in its severity and strength, so that whoever reflects and understands might have an opportunity for repentance. But alas, as happened before, the people blasphemed God instead of offering repentance to Him. This shows the hardness of people's hearts and their ingratitude in the last time.

16.17.3.en: If tribulation comes upon you, beware of murmuring, and examine yourself lest it be because of your sin and your negligence or failing in your relationship with God, for God allows all things for your good and for the completion of your repentance. And if it is not because of your sin, accept it as a divine dispensation that helps you to cling to Him, and even if you do not understand now, your acceptance of it will cause God to explain it to you afterward, and then you will be able to understand. Babylon the harlot and the beast: a general introduction: the coming three chapters deal with one idea, which is the fall of Babylon and the proclamation of heaven's victory. In chapter seventeen we find a description of wicked Babylon and her relation to the beast, in chapter eighteen a description of her fall, and in chapter nineteen the proclamation of heaven's victory .. Perhaps many ask why Babylon, and what is her story, and what are her symbols?..! So here, dear reader, is some information about Babylon and her story in the Holy Bible ..

16.17.4.en: 1- She was called Babel "because the LORD did there confound the language of all the earth" (Gen 11:9), when they wanted to build a tower after the Flood to take shelter in it and to reach heaven. So it is a place that signifies pride and defiance, and it deserved God's punishment.

16.17.5.en: 2- This city was founded by a man named Nimrod (Gen 10:9), whom the Scripture describes as mighty, and he led many to disobey God.

16.17.6.en: 3- This city was famous for the worship of idols and images, and the most famous of its gods was "Marduk," who symbolizes Satan.

16.17.7.en: 4- It was one of the cities to which the people of God were carried captive and which enslaved them for a time, a strong reference to the kingdom of Satan, which fights and takes captive many of the children of God.

16.17.8.en: 5- Just as Jerusalem was a great city because it points to God's dwelling with men, so Babylon also became a great city, as the Book of Revelation described her, because she represents the dwelling of the great Satan in evil, with all his powers and the wicked men who follow him.

16.17.9.en: In sum, Babylon signifies Satan (the Antichrist) and his kingdom, and likewise signifies the company of the wicked, lovers of the world and its desires and its false and passing wealth, and in every case she signifies the state of constant enmity with God ..
